title: CLR/39/2016 of Arsh Bari Vs The Himalaya Drug Company AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
 Civil Revision No. 39 of 2016
 (Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure)
Arsh Bari .......Revisionist
 Vs.
The Himalaya Drug Company & Ors. .........Respondents
Mr. Piyush Garg, Advocate for the Revisionist
Mr. Vivek Pathak, Advocate holding brief of Mr. Ashish Sinha, Advocate for
the Respondent.
List of cases referred:
1. (2011) 8 SCC 670; State of Uttaranchal and another v. Sunil Kumar Vaish
2. 2000 (1) SCC 711; B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai and
Another
3. 1991 Supp(1) SCC 414; State of West Bengal v. Atul Krishna Shaw and
another
Hon'ble Lok Pal Singh, J.
 Present Civil Revision is directed against order
dated 19.02.2016 passed by the 7th Additional District
Judge, Dehradun in O.S. No. 374 of 2009, Himalayan Drug
Company v. Azhar Mohammed and others, whereby the
application paper no. 244 C filed by the revisionist under
order 9 Rule 7 of The Code of Civil Procedure (for short,
CPC) has been dismissed.
2. Factual matrix of the case is that respondent no.1
Company filed a suit against Azhar Mohammed,
predecessor-in-interest of the revisionist, and proforma
respondents for a decree of mandatory injunction,
prohibitory injunction and recovery of damages in respect
of the property in suit. Said suit was registered as O.S.
No.374 of 2009.

2
3. Defendant no.1 appeared before the trial court and
he filed his written statement. Summon were also issued to
other defendants i.e. defendant nos.2 to 7, but the same
were not served. Steps were also not directed to be taken to
serve the defendants through registered post. The
respondent no.1 moved an application before the trial court
seeking permission for substituted service by way of
publication, which was allowed by the court and
straightaway the plaintiff/respondent no.1 was permitted
to take steps for effecting service upon defendant nos.2 to
7 through publication in a in daily local newspaper.
Despite service through publication, defendant nos. 2 to 7
did not appear before the trial court and thus the suit was
proceeded ex-parte against them vide order dated
04.08.2011.
4. On 02.04.2012, defendant no.1 Azhar Mohammed
died. Upon his death, notices were issued to his legal heirs
including the revisionist, defendant no. 2 to7 in the suit,
for substitution. The revisionist on service of notices
appeared before the court below on 14.05.2013, being
oblivious of the fact that by order dated 04.08.2011 the
case has been directed to be proceeded ex parte against
him, being defendant no.7 in the suit. Meanwhile, two
amendment applications were filed by the
plaintiff/respondent no.1 for substitution of the legal heirs
of defendant nos.1 and 2, as it was also brought on record
that defendant no.2 had died prior to institution of suit.
Said amendment were allowed by the trial court vide order
dated 06.01.2014.
5. Subsequently, on inspection of record,
revisionist/defendant no.7 came to know that the suit has
proceeded ex parte against him vide order dated

3
04.08.2011. Therefore, on 26.11.2015, the revisionist filed
an application under order 9 Rule 7 of C.P.C. stating that
after death of his father, on the amendment application
filed by the plaintiff, notice was served upon him.
Thereafter, he appeared before the trial court but he was
not aware of the order dated 4.8.2011. It was also stated
that he could not get the knowledge of the service made
through publication. The Trial Court, vide impugned order
dated 19.02.2016, dismissed the application moved by the
revisionist/defendant no.7 under Order 9 Rule 7 of CPC,
on the ground that the defendant has neither shown a
satisfactory reason for moving the application belatedly nor
has shown a good cause for his non-appearance on date
fixed. In support of his application, the revisionist had
cited following judgments before the trial court: Lal
Bahadur v. 2nd Upper Munsiff Fatehpur and others (AIR
2002 All 360), Delhi Development Association v. Shanti
Devi and others (AIR 1982 SC 159) and Raghuvar v.
.Revenue Council (1998), but the trial court held that
aforesaid judgments are not applicable to the case of the
revisionist/plaintiff.
6. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the entire material available.
7. Perusal of record would reveal that respondent
no.1/plaintiff instituted the suit against the defendants
wherein revisionist was impleaded as Defendant no. 7.
Notices were issued to defendants. Defendant no. 1
appeared before the trial court and contested the suit.
Except defendant no.1, neither any other defendant was
served nor appeared before the trial court. Admittedly, the
service was effected upon the revisionist/defendant no.7 by
means of publication. By order dated 04.08.2011, the trial

4
court held that the service is sufficient upon defendant
nos.2 to 7 through publication, but while doing so, no
satisfaction has been recorded by the trial court in
permitting the respondent no.1 for substituted service.
Order V Rule 20 of CPC would be relevant for the purpose,
which is extracted hereunder:
 20. "Substituted services"
(1) Where the Court is satisfied that there is reason
to believe that the defendant is keeping out of the
way for the purpose of avoiding service, or that for
any other reason the summons cannot be served in
the ordinary way, the Court shall order the summons
to be served by affixing a copy thereof in some
conspicuous place in the Court-house, and also
upon some conspicuous part of the house (if any) in
which the defendant is known to have last resided or
carried on business or personally worked for gain, or
in such other manner as the Court thinks fit.
(1A) Where the Court acting under sub-rule (1)
orders service by an advertisement in a newspaper,
the newspaper shall be a daily newspaper circulating
in the locality in which the defendant is last known
to have actually and voluntarily resided, carried on
business or personally worked for gain.
(2) Effect of substituted service-Service substituted
by order of the Court shall be as effectual as if it had
been made on the defendant personally.
(3) Where service substituted, time for appearance to
be fixed -Where service is substituted by order of the
Court, the Court shall fix such time for the
appearance of the defendant as the case may
require.
8. A plain language of the provisions of Order V
Rule 20 of C.P.C. makes it crystal clear that before passing
any order for substituted service, the court is required to
be satisfied that there is reason to believe that the
defendant is keeping out of the way for the purpose of
avoiding service or that for any other reason, the summons
cannot be served in the ordinary way. Substituted service
is an exception to the normal mode of service. The Court
must apply its mind to the requirements of Order V Rule

5
20 and its order must indicate due consideration of the
provisions contained in it. Evidently the trial court has
failed to apply its mind to the requirements of Order V Rule
20 and has passed the order in a mechanical manner. The
court should be vigilant that the substituted service may
be managed by the plaintiff which may deny fair
opportunity to the defendant.
9. In the instant case, from the perusal of the
record, it transpires that the court has not recorded its
satisfaction before passing the order of substituted service.
That part, order dated 04.08.2011 does not reflect as to in
which newspaper publication was made. There is no
whisper in the orders of the trial court which may suggest
that ever the trial court has recorded its satisfaction that
defendant no. 2 to 7 are avoiding the service of summons
upon them or that the service of summons in ordinary way
is not possible upon them. In such contingency only, the
court can order the summons to be served through
publication or by affixing the notice at the conspicuous
place/ court house and at the house where the defendant
resides lastly or published in a daily newspaper, circulating
in the locality in which the defendant is last known to have
resided or work for personal gain and not in any other way.
In the present case, there is absolutely non-compliance of
Order V Rule 20 of CPC, thus, it cannot be held that the
defendant no.7 was served sufficiently. That being the
position, there was no occasion for the trial court to
presume that the defendant no.7 did not appear, despite
sufficient service, but the trial court did not consider this
legal aspect of the matter and directed the suit to be
proceeded ex-parte against defendant no.7.

6
10. A perusal of impugned order dated 19.02.2016
would reveal that trial court has not discussed any of the
judgment cited by either parties and in a very cryptic
manner has observed that the judgments are not
applicable to the facts of the present case. It was also
observed by the trial court that insofar as the case of
Prahlad Singh is concerned, as per the ratio of law laid
down in that judgment, the application is liable to be
dismissed. The Trial Judge should have discussed the case
laws cited before her to some extent on the facts and the
ratio of laws laid down by the respective High Courts but
no discussion has been made in regard to the fact or the
law. In the impugned order, the Trial Judge has not
recorded any reason to arrive on the conclusion that the
application is liable to be dismissed. It is settled position in
law that recording of reasons is an essential element of
administration of justice. Right to reason is an
indispensable part of sound judicial system and reflect the
application of mind on the part of the court. The purpose of
reasoning in a decision is not only vital for the purposes of
showing the litigant that he/she is receiving the justice but
also a valid discipline for the court itself. The statement of
reasons is one of essentials of justice. In other words,
reasoning of decision of an administrative, quasi-judicial or
judicial authority necessary and life in law.
11. Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Sunil Kumar
Vaish1 has held as under:-
 "19. Judicial decisions must in principle be reasoned and the
quality of a judicial decision depends principally on the quality
of its reasoning. Proper reasoning is an imperative necessity
which should not be sacrificed for expediency. The statement of
reasons not only makes the decision easier for the parties to
understand and many a times such decisions would be
accepted with respect. The requirement of providing reasons

7
obliges the judge to respond to the parties' submissions and to
specify the points that justify the decision and make it lawful
and it enables the society to understand the functioning of the
judicial system and it also enhances the faith and confidence of
the people in the judicial system."
12. In Atul Krishna Shaw3
, Hon'ble Apex Court
has held as under:-
"11. The contention of Shri Chatterjee that it is the duty of
the appellant to produce the record to repudiate the
findings recorded by the appellate authority is without
sub- stance. In a quasi-judicial enquiry is for the parties
who relied upon certain state of facts in their favour have
to adduce evidence in proof thereof. The proceedings
under the Act are not like a trial in a Civil Court and the
question of burden proof does not arise. In the absence of
abduction of the available documentary evidence, the
necessary conclusion drawn by the Asstt. Settlement
Officer that the loan application made might pertain to
plot Nos. 2201 and 2235 is well justified. The appellate
authority is not justified in law to brush aside that
finding. The other finding that the witnesses examined on
behalf of the respondents support the existence of the
fishery for a pretty long time is also without discussing
the evidence and assigning reasons in that regard. The
Asstt. Settlement Officer extensively considered the
evidence and has given cogent reasons which were neither
discussed nor found to be untenable by the appellate
authority. Thus, we have no hesitation in coming to the
conclusion that the Appellate Tribunal disregarded the
material evidence on record, kept it aside, indulged in
fishing expedition and crashed under the weight of
conjectures and surmises. The appellate order is,
therefore, vitiated by manifest and patent error of law
apparent on the face of the record. When so much is to be
said and judicial review done, the High Court in our
considered view, committed error of law in dismissing the

8
writ petition in limine. In the facts and circumstances of
this case, in particular, when the litigation has taken well
over 28 years till now, we find it not a fit case to remit to
the High Court or Tribunal for fresh consideration."
13. As far as the ex-parte order is concerned, it is a
well settled principle of natural justice that no one should
be condemned unheard. The Trial Court should be liberal
in allowing the application for setting aside the ex-parte
order and efforts should be made to decide the matter on
merit, instead of dismissing the same on technicalities. The
provisions of the code are handmaid of justice and the
technicalities should not be permitted to hamper the court
in the administration of justice. It is the duty of the courts
to decide the lis on merit instead of adopting the
technicalities. Reference may be made to B.K. Narayana
Pillai2 in which it has been held by the Apex court that
technicalities of law should not be permitted to hamper the
courts in the administration of justice between the parties.
14. Record reveals that the suit is at preliminary
stage and the issues are yet to be framed. In such a
situation, the Trial court should have been more liberal in
allowing the application for setting aside the ex-parte order
passed against the defendant. Having said so, this Court is
of the firm opinion that the trial court has committed
illegality in dismissing the application moved by the
revisionist. Impugned order is unsustainable in the eyes of
the law and is liable to be dismissed.
15. For the reasons recorded above, instant civil
revision is allowed. Impugned order dated 19.02.2016 is
hereby set-aside. Application paper no.244C is allowed. As
the suit is quite old, trial court is directed to expedite the

9
proceedings of the suit and to decide the same, as
expeditiously as possible, in accordance with law, after
giving ample opportunity of hearing to all the parties. It is
clarified that unnecessary adjournments shall be avoided
and the parties shall cooperate for expeditious disposal of
the suit.
